title: Apostrophes for possession
keyIdea: An apostrophe and s ('s) show that something belongs to someone. Write the owner, then the apostrophe, then s, then the thing: the dog's bone, the girl's hat, Sam's kite. Do not use an apostrophe just because a word ends in s. Three cats means more than one cat, so it has no apostrophe.

kid: The dog has a bone. The bone belongs to the dog. We can write that the short way: the dog's bone.
The little mark is called an apostrophe. Write the owner first: dog. Then put the mark, then s: dog's. Then write the thing: bone.
Not every s needs the mark. Three cats ran means more than one cat. Nothing belongs to them, so there is no apostrophe. The cat's bed is the bed that belongs to the cat, so it has 's.
To find the owner, look for the word with 's. In Mia's cat, Mia has the 's. So the cat belongs to Mia.
adult: This is the possessive apostrophe with singular nouns. It is taught in Year 2 of the English National Curriculum (2014) as 'apostrophes to mark singular possession in nouns', for example the girl's name. In the US it sits in the Common Core Language standards for Grade 2 (L.2.2c: contractions and frequently occurring possessives). Plural possession (the girls' coats) comes later, in Year 4, so this lesson keeps to one owner.

The rule for one owner is always the same: write the whole noun, add an apostrophe, then add s. It works for names (Sam's), common nouns (the man's) and nouns that already end in s (the bus's door, James's bag; some style guides allow James'). The 's makes the noun possessive, and the owner comes before the thing owned: Ben's hat, never hat's Ben.

Common mistakes: an apostrophe in a plain plural (two apple's, often called the greengrocer's apostrophe); the mark after the s for one owner (the dogs' bone, which means more than one dog); leaving it out (the girls bag); and splitting the name (Sa'ms). Be careful with its. The possessive its (the dog wagged its tail) has no apostrophe, because it's always means it is. That is a contraction, a different use of the same mark.

In the lab your child drags the apostrophe into the gap between the owner and the s. Then they sort plain plurals from belongs-to words, read a phrase to find the owner, fix missing and wrong apostrophes, and squash 'the hat that belongs to Ben' into Ben's hat.

familyTip: Go round the house naming things with 's: Dad's mug, the cat's bowl, Nana's chair. Write two or three on sticky notes together, and ask: who is the owner? Where does the mark go?

visual.caption: Does it need an apostrophe? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: drag the apostrophe into the right gap, sort plurals from belongs-to words, find the owner, fix mistakes and say it the short way.

practice.prompt: The ball belongs to the boy. Which is right?
practice.hint: Write the owner first: boy. Then the mark, then s.
practice.explain: One boy owns the ball, so write boy, then the apostrophe, then s: the boy's ball.

practice.prompt: A list has {a} words that mean more than one, like cats. It has {b} words that show something belongs, like the cat's bed. How many words need an apostrophe?
practice.hint: Words that only mean more than one do not need the mark. Count only the belongs-to words.
practice.explain: Only the {b} belongs-to words need 's. The {a} words that just mean more than one need only s.

practice.prompt: Which one means more than one cup, with nothing belonging?
practice.hint: More than one is just s. Is anything owned here?
practice.explain: Two cups means more than one cup. Nothing belongs to the cups, so there is no apostrophe.

practice.prompt: Mia's box has {n} pens in it. She gives {k} of them to Leo. How many pens are left in Mia's box?
practice.hint: Mia's box is the box that belongs to Mia. Start with {n} and take away {k}.
practice.explain: {n} take away {k} is {=n-k}, so {=n-k} pens are left in the box that belongs to Mia.

pool.prompt: In Tom's coat, who owns the coat?
pool.hint: Look for the word with 's. That word is the owner.
pool.explain: Tom has the 's, so Tom is the owner. The coat belongs to Tom.

pool.hint: One sentence shows a hat that belongs to a girl. One has the mark where nothing belongs.
pool.explain: The girl's hat shows the hat belongs to the girl. In 'The girl's like hats' nothing belongs, so it should be girls.

pool.prompt: Say it the short way: the bed that belongs to Kim.
pool.hint: The owner comes first, then 's, then the thing.
pool.explain: Kim is the owner, so Kim's comes first, then the thing: Kim's bed.

pool.prompt: Where does the apostrophe go to show the bone belongs to one dog?
pool.hint: Write all of the owner word first, then the mark, then s.
pool.explain: Write dog, then the mark, then s: dog's. Putting the mark after the s would mean more than one dog.

pool.prompt: A story has {a} words like dogs that just mean more than one, and {b} words like the dog's that show belonging. How many words do not need an apostrophe?
pool.hint: Words that only mean more than one need s but no mark.
pool.explain: The {a} words that just mean more than one take no apostrophe. Only the {b} belonging words need 's.

pool.prompt: Ben wrote: I ate two apple's. What is the mistake?
choices: Two apples just means more than one, so no apostrophe
pool.hint: Does anything belong to the apples?
pool.explain: Nothing belongs to the apples. More than one apple is just apples, with no mark.

pool.prompt: Which one needs an apostrophe added? The ___ tail is long.
pool.hint: The tail belongs to the cat. How do you show that?
pool.explain: The tail belongs to the cat, so write cat's: the cat's tail is long.

pool.prompt: Sam's bag has {n} books. He puts in {k} more. How many books are in Sam's bag now?
pool.hint: Sam's bag is the bag that belongs to Sam. Add the new books.
pool.explain: {n} add {k} is {=n+k}, so the bag that belongs to Sam now has {=n+k} books.
